subject: mathematics
question_text: If sin θ = a/(b + c), then show that cos θ = (2√(bc)/(b+c)) cos(A/2).

mark_split.label: Expand and use the cosine rule

steps.label: Square the given relation
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The sine is given this time, so cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ. Everything else follows the same path as answer 33.

recall.must_convey: That sin θ is squared and cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ formed.

steps.why: sin² + cos² = 1 works in either direction, which is why this twin and answer 33 reach the SAME expression from opposite starting points.

steps.label: Expand and use the cosine rule
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. Identical to answer 33 from here — expand, group, and apply the cosine rule.

recall.must_convey: That the expansion is grouped so b² + c² − a² can be replaced by 2bc cos A.

steps.label: Introduce the half angle
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. 1 + cos A = 2cos²(A/2), the same half of the pair as answer 33.

accept: one plus cos A is two cos squared half A giving four b c cos squared half A

steps.why: A PLUS sign in front of cos A always means the cosine half-angle form. That single observation picks the right identity every time in this family.
common_mistakes: Reaching for the sine half-angle form.

steps.label: Take the square root
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Same finish, and the same answer as answer 33 — which is worth noticing rather than doubting.

recall.must_convey: That the square root gives cos θ = (2√(bc)/(b+c)) cos(A/2).
